questions.stem:
A 6-year-old girl who has never been vaccinated returns from a long visit with relatives abroad with 3 days of sore throat, low-grade fever, and a hoarse voice. Her neck is swollen. A gray, adherent membrane covers both tonsils and the posterior pharynx, and it bleeds when scraped. Gram stain of material beneath the membrane shows gram-positive rods. An electrocardiogram shows new conduction abnormalities.

In addition to an antibiotic such as penicillin, which treatment should she receive?
choices: Intravenous immunoglobulin with high-dose aspirin
Inactivated whole-cell vaccine given today in clinic
Oral rifampin for 4 days for her and her household
Antitoxin directed at the bacterial exotoxin
Vitamin A supplementation

explain.html:
A gray adherent pseudomembrane on the pharynx and tonsils with gram-positive rods in an unvaccinated child is diphtheria, caused by toxigenic Corynebacterium diphtheriae acquired in the nasopharynx. Its exotoxin inhibits cellular protein synthesis, destroying local tissue to form the pseudomembrane, and spreads to distant organs; myocarditis is the most frequent fatal complication, which fits her new conduction changes.

Because the damage is done by the toxin, treatment is diphtheria antitoxin to neutralize toxin that has not yet bound cells, together with penicillin (or erythromycin) to eliminate the organism. Prevention is the routine DTaP series.
why: Immunoglobulin with aspirin treats Kawasaki disease, a vasculitis, not a toxin-producing infection.
Vaccinating during active disease does not neutralize the toxin already causing damage.
Rifampin is used as prophylaxis for contacts of Haemophilus influenzae type b disease.
Vitamin A improves outcomes in measles, not diphtheria.
explain.takeaway: Diphtheria (pharyngeal pseudomembrane, myocarditis) is caused by a protein synthesis-inhibiting exotoxin and is treated with antitoxin plus penicillin.
explain.subject: Immunology

questions.stem:
A 45-year-old farmer stepped on a rusty nail in his barn 10 days ago and did not seek care. His last vaccine of any kind was in childhood. He now has jaw stiffness so severe he cannot open his mouth, a stiff neck, trouble swallowing, and a board-like abdomen. Loud noises trigger painful generalized spasms. He is fully alert.

The toxin responsible for his symptoms acts by which of the following mechanisms?
choices: Inhibiting protein synthesis in muscle fibers
Blocking inhibitory neurotransmitter release centrally
Destroying motor neurons in the anterior horn of the spinal cord
Cross-linking T cell receptors to MHC class II molecules
Binding the acetylcholine receptor at the motor end plate

explain.html:
Trismus (lockjaw), neck stiffness, difficulty swallowing, abdominal rigidity, and convulsive spasms in an alert patient after a puncture wound is generalized tetanus. Clostridium tetani is an anaerobic gram-positive spore-forming rod; spores in soil enter through a wound, germinate in anaerobic conditions, and produce exotoxin.

The toxin binds in the central nervous system and interferes with neurotransmitter release so that inhibitory impulses are blocked. Without inhibition, motor neurons fire unopposed, causing sustained muscle contraction and spasm that can last 3 to 4 weeks. Vaccination with the tetanus component of DTaP and Tdap prevents it.
why: Inhibition of protein synthesis is the action of diphtheria toxin, which causes a pseudomembrane and myocarditis.
Anterior horn destruction is the poliovirus lesion, which causes flaccid, not rigid, paralysis.
Cross-linking T cell receptors to MHC class II is the action of superantigens in toxic shock.
Blocking the acetylcholine receptor would cause weakness, not rigidity and spasm.
explain.takeaway: Tetanus toxin blocks inhibitory neurotransmitter release in the central nervous system, causing unopposed muscle contraction (trismus, rigidity, spasms).
explain.subject: Immunology

questions.stem:
A 16-year-old healthy girl comes for a routine visit. She received one dose of the quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate vaccine against serogroups A, C, W, and Y at age 11. She plans to live in a college dormitory in 2 years. Her mother asks why another meningococcal dose is needed when she was already vaccinated.

Which of the following best explains the recommendation for a booster at this age?
choices: The first dose did not cover serogroup Y
Protection wanes, and the risk peaks in later adolescence
The first dose is given only to prime the response to serogroup B
A booster is required only for travel to the African meningitis belt
A booster is needed only if she has a late complement deficiency

explain.html:
All adolescents receive the MenACWY vaccine at 11 to 12 years. Vaccine effectiveness is high in the first year (about 91%) but falls to about 58% by 2 to 5 years, because protection wanes. A booster at 16 restores protection during the ages when adolescents are at highest risk of meningococcal disease.

Serogroup B is covered by a separate vaccine (MenB), offered on a shared decision basis at 16 to 23 years and now required by many colleges. Extra series and frequent boosters are reserved for high-risk people, such as those with late complement deficiency or asplenia.
why: MenACWY covers serogroups A, C, W, and Y, including Y.
MenACWY does not cover serogroup B, which needs a separate vaccine.
The booster at 16 is routine for all adolescents, not only for travelers.
Late complement deficiency calls for a more intense schedule, but the booster at 16 is recommended for everyone.
explain.takeaway: MenACWY is given at 11 to 12 with a booster at 16 because protection wanes before the peak-risk years of late adolescence.
explain.subject: Immunology

questions.stem:
A public health student reviews US polio cases. After a live oral vaccine containing all three serotypes was introduced in 1963, wild virus transmission ended, with the last endemic case in 1979. By the late 1990s, however, nearly all remaining paralytic polio cases in the US were linked to the vaccine itself. In 2000 the US switched to a different vaccine and these cases stopped.

Which property of the earlier vaccine explains both its benefit and the problem it caused?
choices: Inactivated virus that had to be given by injection
Only one of the three poliovirus serotypes was included
Antibodies were made in the blood but not in the gut
A recombinant viral surface protein made in the laboratory
Live virus shed in stool that rarely caused paralysis

explain.html:
The live attenuated oral polio vaccine contains all three vaccine serotypes and is shed in stool for up to 6 weeks after vaccination. That shedding spreads vaccine virus to contacts and created herd immunity, which helped end wild virus transmission. Rarely, though, the live vaccine virus causes vaccine-associated paralytic polio (VAPP), damaging anterior horn motor neurons as wild virus does.

Once wild polio was gone, VAPP was the main source of paralytic cases, so in 2000 the US switched exclusively to the inactivated polio vaccine (IPV), which cannot cause paralysis and makes more than 99% of recipients immune after 3 doses.
why: The earlier vaccine was oral and live; inactivated injected vaccine is what replaced it.
The oral vaccine contained all three serotypes, not one.
Gut immunity and spread to contacts were strengths of the oral vaccine, not its weakness.
A recombinant surface protein describes the hepatitis B vaccine antigen, not polio vaccine.
explain.takeaway: Live oral polio vaccine gave herd immunity through stool shedding but caused vaccine-associated paralytic polio, so the US uses inactivated polio vaccine only.
explain.subject: Immunology

questions.stem:
An 18-week-old boy is seen for his first well visit since birth; the family missed the 2-month visit after a move. He is healthy and growing well. The clinician reviews the live oral vaccine that protects against the most common cause of severe watery diarrhea, dehydration, and metabolic acidosis in infants, a segmented double-stranded RNA virus that replicates in the small intestinal epithelium.

Which of the following is correct about this vaccine for this infant?
choices: Give the first dose today and complete the series before 2 years
Do not start it; the first dose must come before 15 weeks
Give it only after he turns 12 months, with the measles vaccine
Give an inactivated injectable form instead of the oral vaccine
Start the series today, because there is no upper age limit

explain.html:
The virus described is rotavirus, a segmented double-stranded RNA virus of the Reoviridae family, spread fecal-orally and replicating in small intestinal epithelium. Before the vaccine it infected nearly every child by age 5 and caused more than 500,000 diarrheal deaths a year worldwide.

The vaccine is a live oral vaccine given routinely to all infants, with timing limits: the first dose must be given before 15 weeks of age, and all doses should be finished before 8 months. This 18-week-old is past the window to start the series.
why: The series must be completed before 8 months, and it cannot be started after 15 weeks.
Rotavirus vaccine is an infant vaccine, not one given at 12 months with MMR.
The routine rotavirus vaccine is live and oral; no injectable form is used.
There is an upper age limit: start before 15 weeks, finish before 8 months.
explain.takeaway: Rotavirus vaccine is live and oral; the first dose must be given before 15 weeks and the series finished before 8 months.
explain.subject: Immunology

questions.stem:
A 12-year-old boy comes for his routine adolescent visit. His father asks how the human papillomavirus vaccine can protect against cancer if it does not contain any virus that can infect cells. The clinician explains that the vaccine is made by recombinant technology from one viral protein that assembles by itself into a particle that looks like the virus.

Which of the following best describes the vaccine antigen and how it protects?
choices: E6 and E7 oncoproteins that teach T cells to kill tumor cells
Live attenuated virus that establishes a harmless latent infection
L1 capsid protein particles that induce neutralizing antibodies
Killed whole virus that is effective even in people already infected
A capsular polysaccharide linked to a carrier protein

explain.html:
The HPV vaccine antigen is L1, the major capsid protein, made by recombinant technology. L1 proteins self-assemble into virus-like particles that are noninfectious and non-oncogenic because they contain no viral DNA. The particles look like the real virus to the immune system and induce antibodies that block infection by the vaccine types.

The 9-valent vaccine includes the high-risk types 16 and 18, which cause about 70% of cervical cancers, and types 6 and 11, which cause about 90% of genital warts. Because it prevents infection rather than treating it, there is no evidence of efficacy against a vaccine type the person is already infected with, which is why it is routinely given at 11 to 12 years.
why: The vaccine does not contain the E6 and E7 oncoproteins; it is built from the L1 capsid protein.
The HPV vaccine is not live, and it does not establish any infection.
The vaccine is not a killed whole virus and shows no efficacy against types already acquired.
A polysaccharide linked to a protein describes conjugate bacterial vaccines such as the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine.
explain.takeaway: The HPV vaccine is recombinant L1 capsid protein that self-assembles into noninfectious virus-like particles, preventing (not treating) infection with vaccine types.
explain.subject: Immunology

questions.stem:
A healthy 12-month-old girl is due for her first doses of the live attenuated measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine and the varicella vaccine. Her mother asks whether one combined injection of all four (MMRV) is better than two separate injections at the same visit. The clinician reviews data showing about 8 febrile seizures per 10,000 children aged 12 to 23 months after the combined product, compared with about 4 per 10,000 after separate MMR and varicella vaccines given the same day.

Which recommendation fits these data?
choices: Delay both vaccines until she is 4 years old
Give separate MMR and varicella vaccines for this first dose
Give MMR now and varicella only after age 13
Give the combined vaccine, as seizures are equally common
Give only the measles component now, the rest at 18 months

explain.html:
MMR and varicella vaccines are live attenuated virus vaccines given at a minimum age of 12 months, in a 2-dose series at 12 to 15 months and 4 to 6 years. A combined MMRV product exists, but after the first dose in young toddlers it carries a slightly higher risk of febrile seizures than separate injections given at the same visit.

For that reason, between 12 and 47 months, separate MMR and varicella vaccines are suggested for the first dose. Delaying vaccination is not the answer, since it leaves the child exposed to measles and varicella.
why: Delaying both vaccines leaves her unprotected against measles and varicella during the years of highest exposure.
Varicella vaccine is routinely given at 12 to 15 months; there is no reason to wait until adolescence.
The data show twice as many febrile seizures with the combined product, so they are not equal.
MMR is given as one combined vaccine; it is not split into separate components.
explain.takeaway: For the first dose at 12 to 47 months, separate MMR and varicella vaccines are suggested because MMRV slightly raises febrile seizure risk.
explain.topic: MMR and varicella: febrile seizure risk
explain.subject: Immunology

questions.stem:
A 30-year-old woman at 34 weeks' gestation comes for a prenatal visit in October. Her first child was hospitalized at 2 months of age with wheezing, fast breathing, and low oxygen from inflammation of the small airways during the winter. She asks what can be done to protect the new baby from the same virus this season.

Which of the following is the most appropriate plan?
choices: A single dose of RSV vaccine for her now, at 32 to 36 weeks
Tdap for her now, since it prevents bronchiolitis in infants
Live attenuated nasal influenza vaccine for the newborn at birth
Two doses of RSV vaccine for the infant at 2 and 4 months
No option, since immunity to the virus cannot be given to infants

explain.html:
The older child's illness was bronchiolitis, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is the leading cause of bronchiolitis and viral pneumonia in young children. It is most dangerous for infants, premature babies, and children with underlying conditions.

Pregnant people should receive a single dose of RSV vaccine between 32 and 36 weeks of pregnancy, in most of the US from September through January, so that maternal antibody protects the newborn. If the mother does not receive the vaccine, a monoclonal antibody is available for the newborn.
why: Tdap in pregnancy protects against pertussis, not RSV bronchiolitis.
Influenza vaccine is not given to newborns (it starts at 6 months) and does not prevent RSV.
The RSV strategy is maternal vaccination or a monoclonal antibody for the newborn, not an infant vaccine series.
Infants can be protected passively, either through maternal vaccination or a monoclonal antibody.
explain.takeaway: RSV protection for newborns comes from a single maternal RSV vaccine dose at 32 to 36 weeks during the season, or a monoclonal antibody for the infant.
explain.topic: RSV: maternal vaccine or infant monoclonal antibody
explain.subject: Immunology

questions.stem:
A healthy 4-year-old girl comes in September for her first-ever influenza vaccine; her parents had declined it in prior years. She has no allergies. The clinician explains that the inactivated injectable vaccine protects against influenza A and B, and that young children with influenza can develop otitis media, croup, bronchiolitis, pneumonia, and neurologic complications.

Which schedule is recommended for her this season?
choices: One dose now, then a dose every 5 years
No dose, since vaccination starts at age 5
Two doses during this first season
One dose now, with no further doses needed
A single dose only if she has asthma

explain.html:
Everyone 6 months and older should receive an annual influenza vaccine, especially children under 5 and children of any age with high-risk conditions. Influenza in young children can be complicated by otitis media, croup, bronchiolitis, pneumonia, and neurologic disease, and infants can present with a sepsis-like illness.

Children younger than 8 years who are receiving influenza vaccine for the first time need 2 doses in that first season. After that, one dose each year is enough.
why: Influenza vaccine is given every year, not every 5 years, because the virus changes.
Vaccination starts at 6 months of age, not 5 years.
A single dose is enough only for children who have already been vaccinated before or are 8 or older.
Annual vaccination is recommended for all children 6 months and older, not only those with asthma.
explain.takeaway: Annual influenza vaccine is for everyone 6 months and older; children under 8 receiving it for the first time need 2 doses that season.
explain.subject: Immunology

questions.stem:
A 5-week-old girl is admitted with episodes in which she stops breathing and turns blue. For 2 weeks she had a runny nose and mild cough, then bursts of rapid coughing followed by vomiting. Her father has had a cough for 6 weeks that he calls a lingering cold. A nasopharyngeal specimen grows a small gram-negative coccobacillus. Her mother received no vaccines during pregnancy.

Which intervention would most likely have prevented this infant's illness?
choices: A dose of pertussis vaccine for the infant at birth
Oral rifampin for the father once his cough began
The 2-month DTaP dose given 3 weeks early
Annual inactivated influenza vaccine for the mother
Tdap for the mother at 27 to 36 weeks of each pregnancy

explain.html:
A catarrhal stage followed by paroxysms of cough with post-tussive vomiting and apnea in a young infant, with a gram-negative coccobacillus on culture, is pertussis from Bordetella pertussis. Infants are at greatest risk of serious complications, including apnea, hypoxia, seizures, pneumonia, and pulmonary hypertension. Adolescents and adults lose immunity without boosting and act as the reservoir, as the father did here.

Infants are too young to have received the pertussis vaccine series, so the strategy is a single dose of Tdap during every pregnancy at 27 to 36 weeks. Maternal antibody then protects the newborn through the first months of life.
why: Pertussis vaccine is not given at birth; protection for the youngest infants comes from maternal vaccination.
Rifampin is used for Haemophilus influenzae type b and meningococcal contacts; pertussis contacts receive azithromycin.
An early 2-month dose would still leave the first weeks of life unprotected, when this infant fell ill.
Influenza vaccine does not protect against Bordetella pertussis.
explain.takeaway: Tdap during every pregnancy at 27 to 36 weeks protects young infants from pertussis, which adults often carry unrecognized.
explain.topic: Pertussis: maternal Tdap to protect the infant
explain.subject: Immunology

questions.stem:
A 14-month-old boy whose parents declined all vaccines has fever, irritability, a bulging fontanelle, and neck stiffness. Spinal fluid shows many neutrophils, low glucose, and small pleomorphic gram-negative coccobacilli. The organism grows on chocolate agar but not on blood agar unless certain supplements are added. He has a 3-year-old sister at home who is also unvaccinated.

The organism requires which growth factors, and what should the sister receive?
choices: Factors V and X; rifampin for 4 days
Cysteine and iron; oral doxycycline
Factors V and X; oral azithromycin for 5 days
Cholesterol; a single dose of penicillin
Cysteine and iron; ceftriaxone for 10 days

explain.html:
Meningitis in an unvaccinated toddler with small gram-negative coccobacilli that grow on chocolate agar is Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib). The organism needs factor V (NAD) and factor X (hematin), which chocolate agar supplies. Its type b polysaccharide capsule caused 95% of invasive disease before the vaccine, and meningitis was the most common result; the mnemonic HaEMOPhilus recalls epiglottitis, meningitis, otitis media, and pneumonia.

Close contacts such as household members and day care contacts of a patient with invasive Hib disease receive rifampin prophylaxis for 4 days. Routine Hib vaccination at 2, 4, 6, and 12 to 15 months has reduced incidence by 99%.
why: Cysteine and iron are not the growth requirements of Haemophilus, and doxycycline is not used for Hib contacts.
The growth factors are right, but azithromycin is the prophylaxis for pertussis contacts, not Hib.
Haemophilus does not need cholesterol, and penicillin is not the prophylaxis for Hib contacts.
Cysteine and iron are wrong, and a 10-day course of intravenous antibiotics is treatment of disease, not prophylaxis.
explain.takeaway: Haemophilus influenzae type b grows on chocolate agar (factors V and X), and close contacts of invasive disease receive rifampin prophylaxis.
explain.topic: Haemophilus influenzae type b: culture and contacts
explain.subject: Immunology

questions.stem:
Investigators compare two pneumococcal vaccines in healthy 6-month-old infants. Vaccine 1 contains purified capsular polysaccharide from 23 serotypes. Vaccine 2 contains capsular polysaccharide from fewer serotypes chemically linked to a nontoxic diphtheria toxin protein. Four weeks after the series, infants given vaccine 1 have barely detectable capsule-specific antibody and no rise after a later booster, while infants given vaccine 2 have high titers of class-switched IgG and a strong booster response.

Which of the following best explains the response to vaccine 2?
choices: Infants make more polysaccharide-specific IgM than adults
Diphtheria toxin directly activates B cells as a superantigen
The polysaccharide is presented on MHC class I to CD8 T cells
The carrier recruits helper T cells for switching and memory
Linkage to protein raises antibody only against diphtheria toxin

explain.html:
Polysaccharide antigens alone stimulate B cells without T cell help. That response is weak in children under 2 years, produces little class switching, and creates no memory, which is why the 23-valent polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) is not effective in young children.

Conjugating the capsular polysaccharide to a protein carrier (the nontoxic diphtheria toxin CRM197) lets B cells that bind the polysaccharide present carrier peptides to helper T cells. T cell help then drives class switching to IgG and memory. That is why the pneumococcal conjugate vaccines are highly immunogenic in infants and are given as a 4-dose series at 2, 4, 6, and 12 to 15 months.
why: Young infants respond poorly to polysaccharide alone, so a larger IgM response does not explain the result.
CRM197 is a nontoxic carrier protein, not a superantigen, and superantigens do not create specific antibody.
Polysaccharides are not presented on MHC class I; the carrier peptides are presented on MHC class II to helper T cells.
The key result is high antibody against the capsule, the part that protects against pneumococcus.
explain.takeaway: Conjugating pneumococcal capsular polysaccharide to a carrier protein recruits T cell help, so conjugate vaccines work in infants while the plain polysaccharide vaccine does not before age 2.
explain.subject: Immunology

questions.stem:
A woman delivers a healthy term boy. Her prenatal labs show the following.

Test: Result
Hepatitis B surface antigen: Positive
Hepatitis B e antigen: Positive
Hepatitis B surface antibody: Negative

Without intervention, most infants in this situation become infected, and nearly all of those infected become chronic carriers at risk of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.

Which of the following should the newborn receive within hours of birth?
choices: Hepatitis B vaccine alone, with a second dose at 1 month
Hepatitis B immune globulin alone, with vaccine at 2 months
Inactivated hepatitis A vaccine together with immune globulin
Hepatitis B vaccine plus immune globulin, at separate sites
No intervention until the infant's own surface antigen is checked

explain.html:
The mother is chronically infected (surface antigen positive) and highly infectious (e antigen positive). Infants of such mothers are infected 70 to 90% of the time, and about 90% of infected infants become chronically infected. Hepatitis B causes chronic hepatitis and cirrhosis and about 80% of hepatocellular carcinomas.

The vaccine is recombinant hepatitis B surface antigen and is given to every newborn within 24 hours. When the mother is surface antigen positive, the infant receives both hepatitis B vaccine for active immunity and hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) for immediate passive protection, at separate sites.
why: Vaccine alone is the plan when the mother is surface antigen negative; an infected mother's infant also needs immune globulin.
Immune globulin without the vaccine gives only temporary protection and delays active immunity.
Hepatitis A vaccine does not protect against hepatitis B and is given starting at 12 months.
Waiting allows infection to establish; prevention must start at birth.
explain.takeaway: Newborns of hepatitis B surface antigen positive mothers receive hepatitis B vaccine plus HBIG at separate sites at birth.
explain.subject: Immunology

questions.stem:
A 9-year-old boy has had 6 months of falling grades, personality change, and clumsiness, and now has sudden jerking movements of his arms several times a day. Spinal fluid shows very high levels of antibody against a virus. As an unvaccinated 8-month-old living abroad, he had an illness with high fever, cough, runny nose, and red eyes, followed by a rash that began on his face and spread downward.

Which of the following would have been the most effective way to prevent this outcome?
choices: Acyclovir given at the time of the infant rash
Two doses of a live attenuated childhood vaccine
Inactivated polio vaccine given in the first year of life
Rifampin prophylaxis given right after his infant illness
Hepatitis B vaccine given within 24 hours of birth

explain.html:
The infant illness, a high fever with cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis followed by a descending rash, was measles. Years later, progressive behavioral and intellectual decline with seizures is subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a rare degenerative central nervous system disease that appears 7 to 10 years after measles, especially when measles occurred in infancy.

There is no antiviral that prevents it. Prevention is the live attenuated measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine in two doses, at 12 to 15 months and 4 to 6 years, with an early dose from 6 months in outbreaks or before international travel, which then still requires the two routine doses.
why: Acyclovir targets herpesviruses and has no effect on measles virus.
Polio vaccine does not protect against measles.
Rifampin is antibacterial prophylaxis and has no effect on a viral infection.
Hepatitis B vaccine prevents hepatitis B, not measles.
explain.takeaway: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis is a late fatal complication of measles, especially in infancy, prevented by two doses of MMR.
explain.subject: Immunology
